column2: Seeing the Pandavas in the battle, the warriors, O king, though held back by your son, went on swiftly, O Bharata.
Duryodhana held back those heroes, consoling them, but no great chariot-warrior there obeyed his order.
Then the son of the king of Gandhara, Shakuni, able in speech, said to Duryodhana, O great king:

Why is the force of the Madras being slain while we look on? This is not right in battle while you stand, O Bharata.
mahabharata:9:17.20	It was agreed that we should fight together; why then do you tolerate the enemy's slaying, O king?
[Duryodhana said:] "I held them back earlier, but they did not heed my word; all these have been slain, having plunged into the Pandava force."
[Shakuni said:] "Heroes, enraged in battle, do not follow their master's order; there is no use in being angry at them; this is not the time to neglect them.
Let all of us go there together, with horses, chariots and elephants, to protect the mighty archers who follow the king of the Madras.
We shall guard one another with great effort, O king." Thus all reflecting, they went where the soldiers were.
[Sanjaya said:] Thus addressed, the king, surrounded by a great force, set out with a lion-roar, making the earth tremble.
Strike! Pierce! Seize! Hit! Cut!—so was the tumultuous noise of your army, O Bharata.
The Pandavas, seeing in the battle the followers of the king of the Madras together, advanced on them, taking the middle position.
In a moment, O lord of men, those followers of the king of the Madras were seen slain in the battle, hand to hand.
Then, as we advanced, the victorious Pandavas, mighty, delighted, raised together a clamour.
Then headless trunks were seen risen everywhere, and a great meteor fell, circling the sun.
The earth was covered with shattered chariots, broken axles and yokes, slain great chariot-warriors and fallen horses.
Horses panting, horses yoked together, were seen with warriors there on the battlefield, O great king.
Some horses dragged chariots with broken wheels in the battle; some took parts of chariots and ranged in ten directions; here and there horses entangled in their traces were seen.
Chariot-warriors falling were seen, O best of men, like siddhas dropped from the sky when their merit is exhausted.
With the brave followers of the king of the Madras slain, and seeing us attacking, the Partha great chariot-warriors,
eager for victory, strikers, advanced with speed, making the noise of arrows mingled with the sound of conches.
Meeting us again, having attained their aims, strikers, shaking their bows, they cried lion-roars.
Then, seeing the great force of the king of the Madras slain and the brave king of the Madras felled in the battle, all Duryodhana's army again turned away.
Slain by the victorious Pandavas, O great king, bewildered, it scattered in the quarters, terrified by firm bowmen.
As merchants on a broken boat in a fathomless ocean, wishing for the farther shore of the boundless, when the brave great soul was slain,
the king of the Madras, O great king, we were terrified, wounded by arrows, helpless, seeking a protector like deer tormented by a lion.
Like bulls with broken horns, like elephants with broken tusks, we withdrew at midday, conquered by the son of Dharma.
Neither to rally the divisions nor to show valour, O king, had any warrior of yours the thought when Shalya was slain.
The grief and fear your warriors felt when Bhishma, Drona and the charioteer's son were slain, that fear and sorrow came upon us even more.
Despairing of victory when Shalya, the great chariot-warrior, was slain, their heroes slain, shattered and cut by sharp arrows, with the king of the Madras slain, O king, those warriors fled in fear.
Some mounted horses, some elephants, others chariots, the great chariot-warriors endowed with speed, and foot-soldiers fled in fear.
Two thousand elephants, mountain-like and striking, fled when Shalya was slain, driven by goads and thumbs.
Those men of yours, O best of the Bharatas, fled from the battle in all directions; as they ran they were seen panting, tormented by arrows.
Seeing them broken, fleeing, dispirited and defeated, the Panchalas and Pandavas, eager for victory, rushed at them.
The roar of arrows, a great lion-roar and a dreadful sound of conches of the brave arose.
Seeing the Kaurava army terrified and fleeing, the Panchalas with the Pandavas said to one another:

Today King Yudhishthira, steadfast in truth, has conquered his foes; today Duryodhana is bereft of his shining royal fortune.
mahabharata:9:18.15	Today let Dhritarashtra, lord of men, hearing that his son is slain, fall senseless to the ground and incur guilt.
mahabharata:9:18.16	Today let him know the son of Kunti, capable among all bowmen; today the ill-minded sinner will reproach himself; today he will remember Kshatta's true word, spoken for his good.
mahabharata:9:18.17	From today on, let him serve the Parthas as a servant; let the king know the sorrow the sons of Pandu have undergone.
mahabharata:9:18.18	Today let that lord of the earth know Krishna's greatness; today let him know the dreadful roar of Arjuna's bow in battle,
mahabharata:9:18.19	and the whole strength of weapons and of arms in the fight; today he will know the terrible strength of Bhima the great soul.
mahabharata:9:18.20	When Duryodhana is slain in the battle, as the asura Maya by Shakra, what Bhimasena did at the slaying of Duhshasana, no other in the world could do besides the mighty Bhima.
mahabharata:9:18.21	Let him today know the valour of the eldest Pandava, hearing that the king of the Madras, hard to bear even for the gods, is slain.
mahabharata:9:18.22	Today he will know the mighty sons of Madri in the battle, when Subala's son the brave is slain and the Gandharas in all.
mahabharata:9:18.23	How could those not win whose warriors are Dhananjaya, Satyaki, Bhimasena, Dhrishtadyumna the Parshata,
mahabharata:9:18.24	the five sons of Draupadi, the sons of Madri, the Pandavas, the mighty archer Shikhandin and King Yudhishthira?
mahabharata:9:18.25	How could those not win whose protector is Krishna, Janardana, protector of the worlds, and whose refuge is dharma?
mahabharata:9:18.26	Bhishma, Drona, Karna, the king of the Madras and hundreds and thousands of other kings and heroes—
mahabharata:9:18.27	who else other than Partha Yudhishthira, whose protector is Hrishikesha, ever the treasure of dharma and fame, could conquer them in battle?
Speaking thus, filled with great joy, the Srinjayas followed your broken men from behind, O king.
The valiant Dhananjaya went at the chariot-force, the two sons of Madri at Shakuni, and the great chariot-warrior Satyaki likewise.
Seeing all of them fleeing, afflicted by fear of Bhimasena, Duryodhana then said to his charioteer, as if smiling:

Partha will not pass me standing bow in hand; drive my horses to the rear of all the army.
mahabharata:9:18.32	For Dhananjaya son of Kunti could not pass me fighting at the rear, as the great ocean cannot pass its shore.
mahabharata:9:18.33	See the great army driven by the Pandavas, charioteer; see the dust of the army risen on every side.
mahabharata:9:18.34	Hear the many dreadful, fearful lion-roars; therefore go slowly, charioteer, and guard the rear.
mahabharata:9:18.35	When I stand in the battle and the Pandavas are held back, my force will quickly rally with vigour.
Hearing those words of your son, worthy of the foremost of heroes, the charioteer slowly urged the gold-covered horses.
Twenty-one thousand foot-soldiers, bereft of elephants, horses and chariot-warriors, giving up life, stood for battle.
Born in many countries, wearing varied-coloured garments, those warriors stood, desiring great fame.
As they met each other there, glad, a great, dreadful and terrifying crush took place.
Then, O king, men of many lands held back Bhimasena and Dhrishtadyumna the Parshata with a four-limbed force.
Other foot-soldiers turned on Bhima alone in the battle, shouting, slapping their arms, delighted, wishing to go to the heroes' world.
Reaching Bhimasena, enraged, arrogant in battle, Dhritarashtra's men roared and spoke no other word; surrounding Bhima in battle they struck him on every side.
Though struck in the battle, surrounded by hosts of foot-soldiers, he did not stir on his chariot seat, like Mount Mainaka.
Those enraged, O great king, set about seizing the Pandava's great chariot, and held back other warriors.
Bhima grew angry in the battle at those surrounding him; he swiftly dismounted from the chariot and stood on foot.
Taking a great mace covered with gold, he slew your warriors like Death with a rod in hand.
The strong Bhima with his mace crushed those twenty-one thousand foot-soldiers, bereft of chariots, horses and elephants.
Having slain that host of men, Bhima of true valour, with Dhrishtadyumna before him, was soon seen again.
The foot-soldiers lay slain on the ground, smeared with blood, like flowering karnikara trees broken by wind.
With garlands of various flowers, wearing various earrings, slain were those of many races, assembled from many countries.
That great force of foot-soldiers, covered with pennants and banners, shone cut down there, dreadful and terrible.
The great chariot-warriors of all the army led by Yudhishthira rushed at your son, the great soul Duryodhana.
Seeing your mighty archers turned away, they did not face your son, as sea-monsters do not face the shore.
We saw that marvellous valour of your son, that the Parthas together could not pass him alone.
Not far from where he had fled, resolved on flight, Duryodhana said to his badly wounded army:

I see no place on earth or among mountains where, if you went, the Pandavas would not kill you; what use is flight to you?
mahabharata:9:18.57	Their force is small and the two Krishnas greatly wounded; if all of us stand here, victory will surely be ours.
mahabharata:9:18.58	But the Pandavas, having offended, will pursue and slay you if you are scattered; standing in the battle is better for us.
mahabharata:9:18.59	Hear, kshatriyas, all who are assembled: when Death kills the brave and the timid alike, what fool who calls himself a kshatriya would not fight?
mahabharata:9:18.60	It is better for us to stand in front of enraged Bhimasena; death in battle is pleasant for those who fight by kshatriya duty; having won, one gains happiness here; slain, great fruit in the next world.
mahabharata:9:18.61	There is no better path to heaven, Kauravas, than the duty of war; slain in battle, one soon enjoys the worlds won.
Hearing his words and honouring them, the kings again followed the Pandavas, the aggressors.
As they swiftly came on, the Parthas, eager for victory, strikers, with their divisions arrayed, went to meet them.
The valiant Dhananjaya advanced in the battle in his chariot, shaking Gandiva, famed in the three worlds.
The two sons of Madri against Shakuni and the mighty Satyaki, delighted, fell upon them with speed where your force was.
Mounting a very great elephant, in rut, mountain-like, proud, like Airavata, a crusher of hosts of foes,
born of the Mahabhadra line, always well honoured by Dhritarashtra's son, well equipped by those who knew the decisions of the scriptures, always to be ridden in battles, O king—

mounting him the foremost king (the Shalva king) became like the sun at the end of night risen; on that best of elephants, O king, he advanced against the sons of Pandu from all sides and tore them with sharp arrows like Mahendra's thunderbolt.
As he loosed arrows in the great battle and sent warriors to Yama, O king, neither his own nor the enemy saw his opening, as the daityas of old that of the thunderbolt-bearer.
The Pandavas, Somakas and Srinjayas all saw that elephant alone ranging by thousands on every side, like Mahendra's elephant near.
The enemy force, being routed, seemed as if pleased on every side; it did not stand greatly in the battle for fear, crushing one another.
Then the great Pandava army, suddenly broken by that king, fled in four directions, unable to withstand the elephant-king's speed.
Seeing it broken by his speed, all the chief warriors of yours honoured that king and blew their conches white as the moon.
Seeing the Panchala king coming suddenly, the lion among kings in the battle swiftly sent that elephant to kill Drupada's son.
He pierced that elephant as it suddenly came with three of the best iron arrows, blazing, sharp, smith-polished, bright as the sun, of fierce speed.
Then the great soul loosed five other sharp chief iron arrows at its temple; pierced by them, the mighty elephant turned and fled in the battle.
Checking that king of elephants as it fled, driven, the Shalva swiftly sent it with goad and hook, pointing at the chariot of the Panchala king.
Seeing the elephant come suddenly, Dhrishtadyumna swiftly took a mace from his chariot, the hero, and went to the ground, his limbs bewildered with fear.
That great elephant suddenly crushed that gold-adorned chariot with horses and charioteer, and, raising it with his trunk, dashed it on the ground.
Seeing the Panchala king's son afflicted by that best of elephants, Bhima, Shikhandin and the grandson of Shini rushed at it with speed.
They suddenly checked its speed with arrows as it charged, and the elephant, held by the chariot-warriors, wavered in the battle, being held back by them.
Then the king rained arrows like the sun spreading its net of rays on every side; slain by them, the floods of chariots all fled there.
Seeing that deed of the Shalva, all the Panchalas, Matsyas, Kekayas and Srinjayas, filling the battle with cries of "Alas", the best of men surrounded the elephant on all sides.
The Panchala king's son, swift, brave, taking a mace like a mountain peak, calmly, O Bharata, slayer of foes, the hero followed the elephant with speed.
Then the strong son of the Panchala king struck hard with his mace the mountain-like elephant, streaming rut, bright as a cloud.
With its temple split, it suddenly roared, vomiting much blood from its mouth, and the mountain-like elephant fell, as a mountain shaken by an earthquake.
While that king of elephants was being felled and a cry of "Alas" rose in your son's army, the hero of the Shinis struck off the Shalva king's head with a sharp broad-headed arrow.
His head cut off in the battle by the Satvata, he fell to the ground with the elephant-king, like a great mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt driven by the lord of the gods.
Seeing that force broken, the great chariot-warrior Kritavarman, brave and mighty, held back the enemy army in the battle.
Those heroes, turning back on seeing the Satvata in the battle standing like a mountain, covered with arrows,
then a battle began of the Kurus with the Pandavas who had turned back, O great king, making death their return.
There was a marvellous fight of the Satvata with the enemy, that alone he held back the unassailable Pandava army.
A great lion-roar of those delighted, friends of one another, for the hard deed done, touched heaven.
Terrified by that sound, the Panchalas, O best of the Bharatas, were followed by the mighty-armed Satyaki, grandson of Shini.
Reaching King Kshemadhurti, the mighty, he sent him with seven sharp arrows to Yama's abode.
As that mighty-armed hero came, shooting sharp arrows, the wise Hardikya swiftly rushed at the bull of the Shinis.
With iron arrows and calf-tooth arrows the great chariot-warriors of the Vrishnis and Andhakas struck each other like delighted elephants.
Hardikya and the bull of the Shinis ranged in many paths and repeatedly hid each other in showers of arrows.
We saw in the sky the arrows of the two lions of the Vrishnis, driven by the force of their bows, like swift locusts.
Meeting that one true-deeded, Hardikya pierced his four horses with four sharp arrows.
The long-armed one, enraged, like an elephant struck with a goad, pierced Kritavarman with eight excellent arrows.
Then Kritavarman, striking Satyaki with three stone-whetted arrows loosed full, cut his bow with one.
Casting aside that cut best of bows, the bull of the Shinis swiftly took another bow with arrows, Shaineya.
Taking that excellent bow, the best of all bowmen, of great valour, wisdom and strength, stringing it,
unable to bear the cutting of his bow by Kritavarman, the enraged atiratha quickly attacked Kritavarman.
Then the bull of the Shinis with ten very sharp arrows killed Kritavarman's charioteer, horses and banner.
Then, O king, the great chariot-warrior mighty archer Kritavarman, seeing his gold-adorned chariot with horses and charioteer slain,
seized with great fury, raised a spear, O revered one, and hurled it with the force of his arm, wishing to kill the bull of the Shinis.
The Satvata in the battle split that spear with sharp arrows and felled it crushed, as if bewildering Madhava; then with another broad-headed arrow he struck him in the chest.
In the battle, Kritavarman, his horses and charioteer slain by Yuyudhana, skilled in weapons, fell to the ground.
When that hero was made chariotless by Satyaki in the duel, a very great fear arose among all the armies.
Great despair arose for your son when Kritavarman was chariotless, his charioteer and horses slain.
Seeing the tamer of foes with horses and charioteer slain, Kripa rushed at the bull of the Shinis, O king, wishing to kill him.
Placing him on his chariot, in the sight of all bowmen, the mighty-armed one quickly carried him away from the battlefield.
With Shaineya triumphant and Kritavarman chariotless, O king, all Duryodhana's force turned away again.
The enemy did not know, with the army covered with dust; yours fled, O king, except King Duryodhana.
Duryodhana, seeing his own force broken close by, swiftly attacked and alone held back all of them.
Enraged, he held back all the Pandavas, Dhrishtadyumna the Parshata, Shikhandin, the sons of Draupadi and the bands of the Panchalas,
the Kekayas, the Somakas and the Panchalas, O revered one, unflurried, hard to approach, with sharp weapons.
Your mighty son stood ready in the battle like a great fire at a sacrifice, purified by mantras, blazing.
The enemy mortals did not advance on him, as on Death in the battle; then Hardikya, mounting another chariot, came up.
The earth was covered with his thousands of arrows, and he drenched the enemy with arrows like streams on mountains.
There was no man among the Pandavas in that great battle, nor horse, elephant or chariot, that was not wounded by his arrows.
Whatever warrior I saw in the battle, O lord of men, was covered with arrows by your son, O Bharata.
As the army was seen covered with dust raised by troops, so it was covered with arrows by the great soul.
We saw the earth made a mass of arrows, O lord of the earth, by Duryodhana, the quick-handed bowman.
Among those thousands of warriors of yours and the enemy, Duryodhana alone was a man, I thought.
There we saw your son's marvellous valour, that the Parthas together could not pass him alone, O Bharata.
He pierced Yudhishthira with a hundred in the battle, O best of the Bharatas, Bhimasena with seventy and Sahadeva with seven.
Nakula with sixty-four, Dhrishtadyumna with five, the sons of Draupadi with seven, and pierced Satyaki; he cut Sahadeva's bow with a broad-headed arrow, O revered one.
Casting aside the cut bow, the glorious son of Madri rushed at the king with another great bow, and in the battle pierced Duryodhana with ten arrows.
Nakula too, the hero, mighty archer, pierced the king with nine dreadful arrows and roared.
Satyaki also pierced the king with a straight-jointed arrow, the sons of Draupadi with seventy-three, the king of dharma with seven, and Bhimasena tormented the king with eighty arrows.
Though covered on every side with masses of arrows by the great souls, he did not stir, O great king, in the sight of the whole army.
All men saw the dexterity, the skill and the valour of the great soul exceed all beings.
Dhritarashtra's men, O king of kings, having gone a short distance and not seeing the king, turned back, armoured.
As they rushed, a dreadful, tumultuous noise arose, like that of the troubled ocean at night in the rainy season.
Reaching the unconquered king in the battle, those mighty archers advanced on the Pandavas, the aggressors.
Drona's son held back enraged Bhimasena in the battle. Then with arrows loosed in all directions, O great king, heroes in the battle did not know the quarters or intermediate quarters.
Those two of cruel deeds, both hard to bear, O Bharata, fought dreadfully, each wishing to repay the other, terrifying the whole world, their skin cut by the bowstring's snap.
Shakuni, the hero in battle, tormented Yudhishthira; having killed his four horses, Subala's son, the lord, strong, roared, making all the armies tremble.
In the meantime the valiant Sahadeva carried away in his chariot from the battle the hero, the unconquered king.
Then, mounting another chariot, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, piercing Shakuni with nine and again with five, roared a great roar, best of all bowmen.
That battle was wondrous and dreadful, O revered one, giving delight to the spectators and attended by siddhas and charanas.
Uluka, of immeasurable spirit, rushed on all sides with showers of arrows at the mighty archer Nakula, arrogant in battle.
So too the brave Nakula in the battle covered Subala's son's son with a great shower of arrows on every side.
Those two heroes there in the battle, sons of noble families, great chariot-warriors, fighting each other, saw each other as having done wrong to one another.
Overcome by rage and indignation, Drona's son, O Bharata, did not sleep at all, but sighed like a serpent.
One who kindles a fire himself and wraps it in his garment and burns, suffering mental pain, is not wise.
The wise one said to his mother, trembling, with joined palms, "I will not kill four of your sons, though they are within my reach."
[Gautami said:] "If this ill deed against you, serpent, was done under another's power, then you too are a cause here; therefore you too are guilty."
If you would permit me to go to the forest of austerity—I find no peace, having caused the slaying of the Grandsire and of Karna, the tiger among men who never fled in the wars.
How is it that the aged king, struck by grief for his sons, having received grief from us, does not die?—so he reflects.
Cranes imitated the cries of owls, and goats imitated the cries of jackals, O Bharata.
There they saw Fire standing before them like a mountain, standing blocking the way, in visible human form.
Seeing that Karna, tormentor of strong foes, I did not follow him; for even Shakra could not conquer us if Karna were with us in battle.
